source.title: Accelerating Large Batch Training via Gradient Signal to Noise Ratio (GSNR)
source.authors: Guo-qing Jiang; Jinlong Liu; Zixiang Ding; Lin Guo; W. Lin

page_placements.theme: Batch-size effects depend on workload, recipe and budget

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including appendices.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether a GSNR-based optimizer changes large-batch generalization using different optimizer interventions and benchmarks.
record.gate_note: The paper reports large-batch results and train/test gaps. It cites prior work on other large-batch methods; those cited results are not extracted as this study's own.
record.test_reason: The study reports held-out image-classification accuracy across batch sizes and optimizers, bearing on V4 and V5. Its fixed-batch train–test-gap comparisons alone do not establish a large-batch penalty.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly accurate: the authors conclude that GSNR-based VRGD accelerates large-batch training, improves final performance and reduces reported train–test gaps. They report extending usable batch sizes for BERT and DLRM and improving ImageNet accuracy. These conclusions should not be read as showing that every large-batch accuracy penalty disappears.
record.recipe_differences: Introduces GSNR-based per-parameter gradient scaling in VRGD optimizers; compares against baseline optimizers under large-batch schedules.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size changes the baseline and VRGD performance; CIFAR10 results show sharp baseline accuracy loss at larger batches, and the reported VRGD advantage grows with batch size. The paper reports linear regression sensitivity to γ and device count k, but those are not claim-version outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: At BERT batch size 64k, VR-LAMB reduces the pretraining loss gap from 0.35 to 0.12; training loss rises from 1.11 to 1.31 while test loss falls from 1.46 to 1.43.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: GSNR-based optimizer adaptation can reduce a train–test loss gap at a fixed large batch size.

fits_no_version.finding: In one-epoch DLRM recommendation training, SGD AUC falls to 0.7787 at 512k versus 0.8014 at 32k, while VR-SGD reaches 0.8013 at 512k.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Large-batch penalties and their mitigation by optimizer adaptation also occur in recommendation models.

record.code_released: Code will be released when published; no URL stated.
record.problems: The paper's ImageNet gap table is flattened and internally inconsistent at 32k: the listed gap values do not match the stated 47.1% reduction. Some baseline optimizer results are cited from prior work rather than reproduced. DLRM reports test AUC but not train metrics or a direct generalization gap.
record.rows_left_out: Table 3 reports ImageNet test accuracies, Table 1 BERT F1 scores, and Table 5 DLRM AUCs for the same comparisons; omitted where the corresponding direct generalization-gap or batch-size outcomes are already captured. The six CIFAR10 batch-size entries are preserved together per optimizer in Table 6 rather than split into individual rows.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Width beyond interpolation and the resulting test-error trajectory.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.

Systematic learning-rate and schedule searches, matched training performance, broader tuning, decoupled weight decay, switching optimizers, and an own-experiment language-model comparison against SGD.

Longer-training interventions and controlled normalization or regularization ablations. BERT's fixed-batch loss-gap comparison does not isolate the batch-size penalty; its downstream F1 comparisons also vary phase-specific schedules.
Dropout interventions, small-data regimes and removal of dropout with weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness measurements and their ranking of generalization gaps.
Removal of highly memorized examples versus random removal.

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source for the claim versions. ImageNet Table 4 is flattened across columns: the extraction's apparent 32k reversal is not reliable evidence of an effect reversal. Cited baselines must remain distinguished from the study's own experiments. Optimizer names throughout the record identify training procedures, not model subjects. No uncertainty estimates establish whether small accuracy differences are significant.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Widening beyond interpolation and its effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Language benchmarks, broad hyperparameter tuning, decoupled weight decay, and switching from Adam to SGD.
The paper does not compare large and small batches under a single fixed epoch budget for every benchmark; it tests BERT, ImageNet, DLRM, and CIFAR-10 with the schedules stated for each.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparisons with norm- or margin-based measures.
Removing memorized examples and measuring resulting test accuracy.

rows.subject: LAMB
rows.operation_detail: Reported training loss, test loss, and generalization gap after BERT pretraining at batch size 64k.

rows.note: The paper reports VR-LAMB's gap as 65.7% smaller; this is the LAMB comparison value.
rows.check: A train–test loss gap at one batch size does not measure the held-out-performance penalty from increasing batch size. These are pretraining losses, not downstream SQuAD losses.

rows.subject: VR-LAMB

rows.check: This measures an optimizer intervention at a fixed batch size. The smaller gap largely accompanies higher training loss; it does not establish that increasing batch size hurts held-out performance.
